source_title: The Crazed KTM X-Bow Is Finally Coming To US Roads
source_excerpt:
Only 30 examples of the X-Bow XA will be sold in the U.S., and prices are expected to start just under $500,000
For almost 20 years, the KTM X-Bow has been unavailable in the U.S. market. The forthcoming introduction of the new X-Bow GT-XA will change that. This limited-edition, road-legal version of the X-Bow is being federalized for local use by KTM partner Carbon Yard and will provide wealthy Americans with one of the most hardcore driving experiences available.
The X-Bow GT-XA is very similar to the GT-XR that's been sold in Europe for several years. Unlike the original X-Bow , the GT-XR and GT-XA have a full windshield and a canopy-style roof, making them slightly more usable on the road. KTM will manufacture just 30 examples of the American-bound GT-XA, with prices expected to start at around $490,000. If the car is swiftly approved for sale in the U.S., customer deliveries should start next year. Orders are now open and require a $50,000 deposit.
The GT-XA is expected to largely mimic the GT-XR , which itself has been upgraded for 2027 with the new Factory 600 package. This model uses Audi's familiar turbocharged 2.5-liter five-cylinder, with a new turbo, intake manifold, and larger intercooler, delivering 592 horsepower. It pairs this sonorous engine with a dual-clutch transmission and a mechanical limited-slip differential driving the rear wheels.
America's X-Bow will be useable on the street
KTM says American models will have several unique touches. These include a new suspension system with adjustable compression and rebound, plus a front-axle lift system. The GT-XA will also offer tire-pressure monitoring, and customers can choose custom materials, colors, trim, and interior stitching. According to the Austrian firm, the GT-XA aims to combine the X-Bow's brilliant track capabilities with extra composure and comfort for the street.
KTM will build each car meticulously by hand at its facility, and owners can spend time with engineers and attend exclusive driving experiences, including at the Red Bull Ring. KTM's exclusive U.S. partner Carbon Yard is handling local operations and will sell the GT-XA through select partners.
Like the European-spec GT-XR , America's GT-XA is built around a lightweight carbon fiber monocoque and is based heavily on the GTX and GT2 race cars that KTM builds. The visual highlight of the car is the jet-fighter-inspired canopy, which lifts up from the bodywork, bringing with it the carbon fiber roof, windshield, and the side windows. Much like a proper race car, the GT-XA will also come standard with fixed seats and uses an adjustable pedal box and steering wheel so owners can find their perfect driving position.
KTM famously fell on hard times in 2024 and went into self-administration while struggling with hundreds of millions of euros worth of debt. The motorcycle arm of the firm was sold to Indian manufacturer Bajaj Auto, and the company behind the X-Bow has been split off into a separate company. It is now being backed by a Belgian investment consortium that includes racing driver Guillaume de Mévius.
